questions.prompt: A skill's command works perfectly from the menu, but it never fires on a natural request. You have already improved the description twice and nothing changed. What is the next move?
options: Add more trigger phrases to when_to_use until the description is longer
Stop editing words and run claude --debug — malformed frontmatter loads the body with empty metadata, which looks identical to a bad description
Set user-invocable: false so Claude is the only caller and picks it up more reliably
Move the markdown body above the frontmatter so it is read first
questions.explanation: Two different causes produce this exact silence: a description that doesn't match human phrasing, and a YAML parse error that leaves metadata empty while the command still loads. Once you've already edited the description twice with no result, the cheap hypothesis is spent — the debug log names the parse error, and the skill's directory name is the other thing to check for a refused character. Option A makes the truncation cap worse without testing a new hypothesis. Option C makes it worse in a different way — it removes your ability to run it directly. Option D inverts the file format.

questions.prompt: You author a skill that commits and pushes to main. It fires on its own during an unrelated refactor, twice in one week. Which frontmatter change addresses the actual failure?
options: deleteModelInvocation is not a field, so the only option is renaming the skill to something less alarming
disable-model-invocation: true, which stops Claude choosing it automatically while you can still run /name — and drops its description from the listing you were paying for
user-invocable: false, which keeps it out of the model as well as the menu
allowed-tools: Bash(git commit:*) so the pushes are pre-approved and stop causing problems
questions.explanation: The failure is automatic invocation of a side-effecting skill, and disable-model-invocation is the field that stops exactly that while leaving /name working — and it also removes the description from the model-visible listing, so you stop paying for a skill that must never self-fire. Option C is close enough to be the tempting wrong answer: user-invocable false hides it from you, leaving Claude as the sole caller, which is the opposite of the intent. Option A invents a field. Option D pre-approves the danger instead of removing the trigger.

questions.prompt: A reviewer complains your skill auto-fires on every file in the repo and only ever makes sense for one of them. Which change expresses that constraint?
options: Rewrite the description so it names the one file type
paths with a glob for that file type, so automatic activation is limited to matching files
Move the skill into a nested .claude/skills directory under that file's project
questions.explanation: paths is the field that limits automatic activation by glob, using the same format as path-scoped rules — it constrains when the skill loads, which is exactly what the reviewer is asking for. Option A is worth doing but it is a softer fix: it makes matching less likely rather than impossible. Option B invents a settings key. Option D changes where the skill is discovered, which affects who gets it, not which files it fires on.
